conflicts/rwanda-genocide/name: The Rwandan genocide and the churches
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/religionRoleNo: The genocide of the Tutsi was not a religious war: killers and victims overwhelmingly shared the same Catholic and Protestant churches, and the organisers' ideology was ethnic and political ('Hutu Power'). Religion's role lies in the churches' long entanglement with the state and with racialised ethnic categories. Historians such as Ian Linden and Timothy Longman show how missionaries and bishops first championed a Tutsi elite under Belgian rule, then from the 1950s backed the 'Hutu revolution', and how senior clergy stayed closely tied to President Habyarimana's single-party regime. Longman argues that church hierarchies taught obedience to authority and tolerated ethnic discrimination, so that many parishioners saw no contradiction between churchgoing and killing; others, including Rwandan Catholic writers, stress that the hierarchy did not plan the genocide, that many clergy were themselves murdered, and that individual Christians of all churches risked their lives to shelter Tutsi. The debate is over the degree of institutional responsibility, not over the fact that churches became killing grounds and that some clergy took part.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/sides/0/name: Interim government, Rwandan Armed Forces (FAR) and the Interahamwe and Impuzamugambi militias ('Hutu Power')
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/sides/0/faith: Overwhelmingly baptised Catholics and Protestants; the ideology was ethnic nationalism, not religion
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/sides/1/name: Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) and its army
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/sides/1/faith: Mainly Tutsi exiles of Christian background; a secular political-military movement
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/sides/2/name: Victims: Tutsi civilians and Hutu political opponents and moderates
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/sides/2/faith: Catholic, Protestant, Adventist and Muslim Rwandans
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/summary: Between April and July 1994 Hutu extremists organised the murder of roughly half a million to 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in about a hundred days. Rwanda was one of the most Christianised countries in Africa, and many of the worst massacres happened inside churches where Tutsi had sought sanctuary; some priests, pastors and nuns helped the killers, while others died protecting the hunted. The genocide forced the Catholic, Anglican, Adventist and other churches into a painful reckoning with their political alliances and their teaching about ethnicity.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/story:
Rwanda's Catholic mission was founded by the White Fathers in 1900, and under Belgian rule after the First World War the church worked hand in hand with the colonial state. Belgian administrators and missionaries such as Bishop Léon Classe treated the Tutsi minority as a natural ruling caste and favoured them in schools and chiefships; ethnic identity cards were introduced in 1933–34. After King Mutara III Rudahigwa's baptism and the dedication of Rwanda to Christ the King in 1946, mass conversion made the country overwhelmingly Christian. In the 1950s a new generation of missionaries, sympathetic to Christian democracy and the Hutu majority, changed sides: the Hutu Manifesto of 1957 was co-written by Grégoire Kayibanda, a former seminarian and editor of the Catholic paper Kinyamateka, and Archbishop André Perraudin's 1959 Lenten letter was read by many as endorsing the Hutu cause. The 'social revolution' of 1959–62 drove tens of thousands of Tutsi into exile, and periodic massacres followed.

Under President Juvénal Habyarimana (1973–94) the churches remained close to the ruling party, the MRND. Archbishop Vincent Nsengiyumva of Kigali sat on its central committee until Vatican pressure obliged him to step down around 1990, and Anglican and some Protestant leaders were similarly tied to the regime. When the Rwandan Patriotic Front, formed by Tutsi refugees in Uganda, invaded in October 1990, the government answered with propaganda against Tutsi as 'inyenzi' (cockroaches), local massacres and the arming of party militias. Some Christian voices, including the journalist-priest André Sibomana and a number of Catholic and Protestant clergy, publicly denounced these abuses; church leaders also helped broker the Arusha Accords of August 1993, which promised power-sharing.

On the evening of 6 April 1994 Habyarimana's aircraft was shot down over Kigali. Within hours the Presidential Guard and militias began killing opposition politicians, including Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana, and Tutsi civilians, using lists prepared in advance. Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines urged listeners to 'work' and leave no Tutsi alive. Local officials, soldiers and the Interahamwe gathered people at roadblocks, communal offices, schools and churches, then killed them with firearms, grenades, machetes and clubs. Sexual violence against Tutsi women was systematic. UN peacekeepers (UNAMIR) were cut to a token force after ten Belgian soldiers were murdered, and outside powers declined to intervene.

Churches, traditional places of refuge in earlier pogroms, became sites of mass murder. At Ntarama and Nyamata in Bugesera thousands were killed inside and around the church buildings in mid-April; at Nyange the parish priest Athanase Seromba was convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) of helping to organise the bulldozing of his church on some 2,000 refugees. The Adventist pastor Elizaphan Ntakirutimana was convicted by the ICTR for his part in the attacks on Mugonero mission, and two Benedictine nuns of Sovu were convicted by a Belgian court in 2001 for complicity in killings at their convent. At the same time Christians of every denomination, and Rwandan Muslims, hid neighbours; among those killed for doing so was Sister Félicité Niyitegeka, who refused to abandon the people she was sheltering at Gisenyi. More than 200 priests, religious and pastors were killed, Tutsi and Hutu alike.

The RPF, led by Paul Kagame, renewed its offensive in April and advanced through the east and centre. Its soldiers also committed reprisal killings of civilians: a 1994 UNHCR mission led by Robert Gersony estimated that tens of thousands died at their hands, and on 5 June 1994 RPF soldiers at Gakurazo near Kabgayi killed Archbishop Nsengiyumva, Bishops Thaddée Nsengiyumva and Joseph Ruzindana and about ten priests. French troops entered the south-west in June under Operation Turquoise. Kigali fell to the RPF on 4 July, and by mid-July the interim government, army and some two million Hutu civilians had fled, largely into Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), where the refugee camps became bases for the defeated forces and the region's later wars.

The UN Security Council established the ICTR at Arusha in November 1994; it convicted the former prime minister Jean Kambanda, Bagosora and others, as well as clergy. Inside Rwanda, mass trials were handled from 2002 by community gacaca courts. Several church buildings, including Ntarama and Nyamata, were turned into national memorials where the victims' bones and clothing are displayed. The relationship between the new government and the churches, especially the Catholic Church, remained tense for years over accusations of complicity and clergy who escaped to Europe.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/nameOfGod: Genocidal propaganda was ethnic rather than theological, but it borrowed religious idiom: extremist media cast the Tutsi as foreign invaders, and some Hutu Power publications and speakers presented the extermination as a duty and even claimed divine favour. Historic Catholic teaching had long been used to legitimise first Tutsi and then Hutu rule, and the hierarchy's public statements in April 1994 called for peace in general terms without naming the genocide or the government. Killers often attended Mass, and some reportedly paused to pray before resuming the slaughter, which survivors and later Rwandan church leaders described as the deepest betrayal of the gospel.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/religiousCause: Missionary and colonial 'Hamitic' theory, taught in mission schools, portrayed Tutsi as alien Nilotic conquerors and Hutu as native Bantu, hardening ethnic categories that propaganda later exploited.
The Catholic Church first sponsored a Tutsi elite and then, from the 1950s, the Hutu counter-elite, so that ethnic politics and church politics became intertwined.
Senior clergy's membership of or closeness to the ruling MRND party compromised the churches' ability to criticise government violence before and during 1994.
A culture of deference to authority, reinforced in church teaching and practice, made it harder for congregations to resist orders from local officials, as Timothy Longman argues.
Previous massacres (1959–63, 1973, 1990–93) had gone unpunished and were seldom forcefully condemned by church hierarchies, which encouraged impunity.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/otherCauses/0: Colonial racialisation of Hutu and Tutsi identities, including the ethnic identity cards introduced by the Belgian administration in 1933–34.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/otherCauses/1: The civil war that began with the RPF invasion of October 1990 and Hutu extremists' fear of losing power under the Arusha Accords.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/otherCauses/2: Economic crisis after the collapse of coffee prices in the late 1980s, land scarcity and structural adjustment.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/otherCauses/3: A centralised, highly organised state with administrative structures down to the hill level that could mobilise the population.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/otherCauses/4: Hate media such as Kangura and Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines, and the arming of party militias.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/otherCauses/5: International passivity, including the reduction of UNAMIR in April 1994 and the reluctance of the UN Security Council to use the word 'genocide'.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/triggers/0: The shooting down of President Habyarimana's aircraft over Kigali on 6 April 1994, which also killed Burundi's president Cyprien Ntaryamira.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/triggers/1: The immediate murder of moderate politicians, including Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana, by the Presidential Guard on 7 April.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/triggers/2: The withdrawal of most UN peacekeepers after the killing of ten Belgian soldiers, which signalled to the organisers that there would be no intervention.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/0/tex: The White Fathers found the first Catholic mission in Rwanda at Save.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/1/tex: Belgian authorities issue identity cards recording each Rwandan's ethnicity as Hutu, Tutsi or Twa.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/2/tex: The Hutu Manifesto, co-written by Grégoire Kayibanda, a Catholic journalist close to the mission, demands an end to Tutsi dominance.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/3/tex: Archbishop André Perraudin's Lenten pastoral letter on charity and justice; the 'Hutu revolution' begins and Tutsi flee into exile.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/4/tex: The RPF invades from Uganda on 1 October; the government responds with mass arrests and local massacres of Tutsi.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/5/tex: The Arusha Accords, supported by church mediators, provide for power-sharing; the UNAMIR peacekeeping force is deployed.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/6/tex: 6 April: Habyarimana's plane is shot down and the genocide begins; in mid-April thousands are killed in the churches of Ntarama and Nyamata.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/7/tex: 5 June: RPF soldiers kill three Catholic bishops and about ten priests at Gakurazo near Kabgayi.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/8/tex: 4 July: Kigali falls to the RPF; in November the UN creates the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/9/tex: A Belgian court convicts two Benedictine nuns of Sovu for complicity in genocide.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/10/te: The ICTR convicts Fr Athanase Seromba over the destruction of Nyange church; his sentence is raised to life imprisonment on appeal in 2008.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/11/te: Rwanda's Catholic bishops issue a formal apology for the part played by members of the church in the genocide.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/timeline/12/te: Pope Francis, meeting President Kagame in the Vatican, asks forgiveness for the 'sins and failings of the Church and its members'.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/0/fo: His 1959 pastoral letter, which condemned social injustice against the Hutu majority, was read as church support for the Hutu revolution.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/0/ou: Remained a respected figure to the post-independence regime and a symbol to critics of the church's ethnic politics.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/1/fo: A close ally of President Habyarimana who sat on the ruling party's central committee; criticised for failing to denounce the genocide clearly.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/1/ou: Killed by RPF soldiers at Gakurazo on 5 June 1994 with two other bishops and several priests.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/2/fo: Convicted of helping to organise the demolition of his church on Tutsi refugees in April 1994.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/2/ou: Fled to Italy and worked as a priest under another name; surrendered to the ICTR in 2002 and was sentenced on appeal to life imprisonment.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/3/fo: Convicted by the ICTR of aiding and abetting the attack on Tutsi who had taken refuge at the Mugonero Adventist complex, in a case that also convicted his son.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/3/ou: Extradited from the United States, sentenced in 2003 to ten years and released shortly before his death.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/4/ro: Hutu religious sister of the Auxiliaires de l'Apostolat
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/4/fo: Sheltered Tutsi at Gisenyi and helped them escape to Zaire; refused her brother's offer of safety unless those with her were spared.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/4/ou: Killed by militiamen on 21 April 1994; honoured by the Rwandan state as a national hero.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/5/ro: Catholic priest and editor of Kinyamateka
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/5/fo: Exposed human rights abuses and corruption before 1994, hid people during the genocide and afterwards also criticised abuses by the new government.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/5/ou: Died in 1998; his interviews were published as Hope for Rwanda.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/6/ro: Commander of the Rwandan Patriotic Army
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/6/fo: Led the RPF offensive that ended the genocide; his forces were also responsible for reprisal killings of civilians and clergy.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/keyPeople/6/ou: Vice-president from 1994 and president of Rwanda from 2000.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/casualties/not: Range for victims of the genocide, overwhelmingly Tutsi. Alison Des Forges (Human Rights Watch, 1999) estimated at least half a million; demographic studies (e.g. Marijke Verpoorten) suggest around 600,000 Tutsi, roughly three-quarters of the Tutsi population; the Rwandan government's 2002 census of victims counted over one million, including Hutu victims. Not included: Hutu killed by the RPF in 1994, which a UNHCR team led by Robert Gersony estimated at roughly 25,000–45,000 between April and August, and the far larger death toll of the subsequent wars in Zaire/Congo.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/effects/0: The RPF took power, ending the genocide and establishing the government that has ruled Rwanda since 1994.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/effects/1: Some two million refugees fled to Zaire, Tanzania and Burundi; armed camps in eastern Zaire helped trigger the Congo wars of 1996–2003.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/effects/2: The ICTR (1994–2015) produced the first international convictions for genocide and recognised rape as an act of genocide (Akayesu, 1998).
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/effects/3: Rwanda's gacaca courts tried well over a million cases between 2002 and 2012.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/effects/4: Ethnic identity cards were abolished and public use of Hutu and Tutsi categories was strongly discouraged by law.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/effectsOnChurc: Churches such as Ntarama, Nyamata and Nyange were left as genocide memorials; many congregations no longer had a building or a pastor.
Hundreds of clergy and religious were killed, and others were tried or fled, leaving church structures devastated.

The Catholic Church's credibility in Rwanda was badly damaged; the government accused it of complicity and of protecting suspects abroad, while the Vatican initially stressed individual rather than institutional guilt.
Rwandan Catholic bishops apologised in 2016 and Pope Francis asked forgiveness in 2017; Protestant churches also issued confessions, notably the Detmold confession of 1996.
Many Rwandans left the historic churches for Pentecostal congregations, and Islam gained respect for the record of Muslim rescuers.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/legacy: The Rwandan genocide is the starkest modern case of mass atrocity inside a predominantly Christian society, and it is studied in seminaries and churches as a warning about church–state alliances, ethnic loyalty and the failure of preaching to shape conduct. It is also remembered for the rescuers, clergy and lay, who died rather than hand over their neighbours.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/dissenters/0/t: A Hutu sister who chose to die with the Tutsi she had been sheltering rather than accept safety for herself alone.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/dissenters/1/t: Priest-journalist who denounced the regime's abuses from 1990, hid potential victims in 1994 and afterwards insisted that all crimes, including the RPF's, be acknowledged.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/dissenters/2/n: Rwandan Muslims of Biryogo and elsewhere
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/dissenters/2/t: Muslim communities widely sheltered Tutsi and refused to join the killing, an example frequently cited by Rwandan Christians in later self-examination.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/dissenters/3/t: In May 1994 he publicly described the killings as a genocide, before many governments would use the word, and called on Catholics not to take part.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/dissenters/4/t: In 2017 asked forgiveness for the sins and failings of the church and its members, 'among whom priests, and religious men and women' who succumbed to hatred and violence.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/theatres/0/nam: Kigali: Sainte-Famille church and Hôtel des Mille Collines
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/theatres/7/nam: Gakurazo: bishops killed by RPF soldiers
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/theatres/9/nam: International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, Arusha
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/campaigns/0/pe: Rwandan Patriotic Army under Paul Kagame
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/campaigns/0/te: From its northern base the RPF pushed south and east, taking Byumba in April, Kabgayi in early June (where the bishops were killed), Gitarama in mid-June and Kigali on 4 July, then swept west to Ruhengeri and Gisenyi, driving the interim government and its army into Zaire by mid-July.
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/campaigns/1/ti: The flight of the interim government and Hutu civilians
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/campaigns/1/pe: Interim government, FAR, militias and some two million civilians
conflicts/rwanda-genocide/campaigns/1/te: The interim government moved from Kigali to Gitarama and then Gisenyi before crossing into Zaire in July, accompanied by a mass exodus of civilians; cholera killed tens of thousands in the Goma camps, which the former army and militias soon controlled.
